module_title: Memory Units - Foundational Basics and Smallest Units
introduction: In the 'Computer Knowledge' section of competitive exams (SSC, Railways, Banking), 'Memory Units and Conversions' is a high-scoring, guaranteed-question topic. At this foundational level, we focus on the smallest units of data and the basic conversion sequence that every candidate must memorize.

core_concepts.title: Bit (The Smallest Unit)
core_concepts.description: A 'Bit' is the smallest unit of data in a computer. The word is an abbreviation for 'Binary Digit'. A bit has a single binary value, either '0' or '1'.

core_concepts.title: Nibble
core_concepts.description: A group of 4 bits is called a Nibble. It is also frequently referred to as a 'Half Byte' in exam terminology. (1 Nibble = 4 Bits).

core_concepts.title: Byte
core_concepts.description: A group of 8 bits is called a Byte. It is the fundamental unit used to represent a single character, number, or symbol (like 'A', '7', or '@') in memory. (1 Byte = 8 Bits = 2 Nibbles).

core_concepts.title: Basic Unit Conversions
core_concepts.description:
Computer memory scales up in standard steps:
- 1 Kilobyte (KB) = 1024 Bytes
- 1 Megabyte (MB) = 1024 Kilobytes (KB)
- 1 Gigabyte (GB) = 1024 Megabytes (MB)

important_entities.name: The Significance of 1024
important_entities.key_fact: Computers operate on Base-2, not Base-10
important_entities.significance: Because computers use the binary system, memory increases in powers of 2. 2 raised to the power of 10 (2^10) equals 1024. This is why 1 KB is exactly 1024 Bytes, not a flat 1000.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: A massive and highly repeated trap! A lowercase 'b' strictly stands for 'bit', while an uppercase 'B' strictly stands for 'Byte'. For example, internet speeds are measured in Mbps (Megabits per second), while file sizes are in MB (Megabytes).
If an exam asks for the 'Smallest unit of computer memory', the answer is ALWAYS 'Bit'. Do not choose Nibble or Byte.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use the first letters to remember the escalating order of memory sizes: K (KB) -> M (MB) -> G (GB) -> T (TB/Terabyte).

exam_strategy_tips: Direct questions like 'How many nibbles are in 1 Byte?' (Answer: 2) or 'What is a half-byte called?' (Answer: Nibble) are extremely common in SSC Tier-1 and CHSL exams. Lock these facts in.
